cases.task: Write the finished README.md for this repository from these verified facts. The current README says: "Patchdeck — powerful, seamless config management. Features: fast diffs, easy workflow, advanced architecture. npm install -g patchdeck. See docs for usage." It is misleading and generic. The audience is developers reviewing changes to JSON configuration before applying them. Patchdeck compares two JSON files locally, shows a field-level diff, and optionally updates the first file to match the second. No data leaves the machine. It is not published to any registry and has no logo, performance measurements or CI badges. The supported path starts in an existing checkout on macOS or Linux with Bun >=1.3.14. Install dependencies using bun install --frozen-lockfile. The shipped command is bun src/main.ts diff <current.json> <desired.json>; default mode never writes. Appending --write overwrites the current file, so use copied inputs for an apply example. There is no --dry-run flag. Existing sample files are examples/current.json and examples/desired.json. Running the default command on these files prints exactly two lines: "~ retries: 2 -> 4" and "~ region: us-east -> eu-west". Existing documentation: docs/format.md explains supported JSON and comparison behavior; docs/options.md contains the full CLI reference; CONTRIBUTING.md has contributor setup and tests; LICENSE contains the MIT license. No other documentation files exist. Source folders are src/ and test/. Produce a concise, distinctive, credible README with a useful first task and only visuals that help the reader. Return only the README Markdown. You have the relevant facts; do not claim to have run commands or inspected a renderer.
success_criteria: Opening concretely identifies JSON configuration review and its useful result; the page demonstrates the actual diff rather than relying on promotional adjectives or repeated feature claims.

The consumer path is complete from the stated existing checkout: Bun/platform prerequisite, bun install --frozen-lockfile, exact supported diff command using shipped examples, and the given expected output appear before contributor or architecture detail.

Explains local processing and default read-only behavior, and clearly states that --write overwrites the current file; any apply example protects shipped input using a copy and the command does not invent --dry-run.

Does not invent registry installation, release availability, logo, badges, measurements, features or documentation links. Finished README prose contains no authoring commentary or false execution/renderer-verification claims.

Page has a clear reading order and purposeful emphasis: useful headings, brief connecting prose, a copyable example and meaningful deeper links; no redundant feature matrix, decorative architecture diagram, empty sections or navigation that overwhelms this small page.

cases.task: Rewrite this confusing developer-doc section into a compact, polished explanation with Mermaid and any other Markdown elements that genuinely help: "Export flow: Client -> API -> Queue -> Worker -> Store -> API -> Client. Everything goes through this pipeline. See code for failures." That linear diagram is wrong. Verified behavior: a client submits an export request to the API. The API checks tenant access before enqueueing. Rejected access returns 403 and no job is enqueued. If the queue rejects the enqueue, the API returns 503. When the queue acknowledges acceptance, the API returns 202 plus job_id immediately; it does not wait for the worker or return a download URL. Later the worker consumes the job and writes its file and final job status to Store, an internal service holding both output files and job status. Worker processing may fail: it retries at most twice after its first attempt; after exhaustion it records failed status. Only after file writing succeeds does it record ready status. The client independently polls GET /jobs/{job_id}. On every poll the API checks tenant access before reading status from Store. A pending job has no download URL, a failed job has an error and no URL, and a ready job returns a short-lived download URL. These checks also apply when the caller knows another tenant's job_id. No timing measurements, specific URL TTL, cancellation, callback or event stream are documented. The destination is GitHub Markdown, read in light/dark modes and at narrow widths. Choose an appropriate diagram type and scope; preserve the distinction between acceptance and completion. Do not force every fact into one giant diagram. Return only the finished section, without claiming tools were run.
success_criteria: Diagram semantics clearly separate request acceptance from background completion: tenant check precedes enqueue, queue acceptance precedes 202 plus job_id, and the API response does not wait for worker output or include a download URL.

Shows or explains both submit rejection paths (403 for access, 503 for failed enqueue) and bounded worker failure (two retries after the first attempt, then failed); does not imply unlimited retries or ready status before file-write success.

Polling is an independent client action with tenant authorization on every request before reading status, including known foreign job IDs; pending and failed have no URL, and only ready returns a short-lived URL.

Uses meaningful labels for actions/conditions and a nearby takeaway, preserves consistent actor names and abstraction, and avoids an unlabeled component chain, excessive diagram density, redundant decoration, or encoding a crucial distinction only in color.

Output is a self-contained developer-doc section with appropriately fenced Mermaid and readable supporting structure; introduces no invented TTL, performance claims, callbacks, cancellation, files, or claims of executed render verification.
